summary: Describes how Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet traffic parameters, as defined in MEF 10.1, can be expressed when using GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling. This lets a requested Ethernet connection state the traffic rates it needs.

eli5.summary: When you order an Ethernet link, you say how much traffic it can carry. This defines how to put that order into the messages that set up GMPLS paths.

questions: what is the ethernet sender_tspec object
what are cir and eir in gmpls
what is the ethernet bandwidth profile tlv
subtitle: How a GMPLS signaling request states the Ethernet traffic rates it needs.

tldr.problem: GMPLS signaling had no way to carry the Metro Ethernet Forum traffic parameters, such as committed and excess rates, when setting up an Ethernet path.
tldr.mechanism: It defines Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects (C-Type 6) holding a switching granularity, an MTU and TLVs, chiefly an Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV with CIR, CBS, EIR and EBS.
tldr.outcome: Ethernet LSPs can request and reserve bandwidth in MEF terms. The RFC updates RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

today: RFC 6003 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
GMPLS lets signaling carry technology-specific parameters (RFC 3471). This document adds Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects to support the Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) traffic parameters of MEF 10.1 and ITU-T Ethernet Service Switching (RFC 6004).

For Ethernet Private Line services the parameters apply to each Ethernet Virtual Connection (EVC) crossing a port. For Ethernet Virtual Private Line services they apply per EVC, with a single or multiple Class of Service, independent of the VLAN IDs. The objects can also signal Ethernet Label Switched Paths (LSPs) more broadly.
sections.eli5: This adds a new form field to the messages that set up network paths, so you can write down how much Ethernet traffic the path should carry.

sections.title: How the Objects and the Bandwidth Profile Fit In
sections.content:
In GMPLS RSVP-TE (RFC 3473), the SENDER_TSPEC object on a Path message says what bandwidth is requested, and the FLOWSPEC object on a Resv message says what was actually reserved. The Ethernet versions carry the link type (switching granularity) and an MTU, with the bandwidth details in a Bandwidth Profile TLV.

The Bandwidth Profile uses the MEF 10.1 parameters. The committed rate is described by CIR (Committed Information Rate, an average rate the network commits to carry) and CBS (Committed Burst Size). The excess rate is described by EIR (Excess Information Rate, an average rate above CIR with no performance objectives) and EBS (Excess Burst Size). The Color Mode says whether the profile is color-aware or color-blind, and the Coupling Flag chooses between two modes of the rate enforcement algorithm.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone plan: a rate you are promised, a bit extra you may use with no promise, and a limit on how big a quick burst can be.

sections.title: The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC Object
sections.content:
The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object has Class-Num 12 and Class-Type 6. After the standard header come a 16-bit Switching Granularity, a 16-bit MTU, and TLVs. There MUST be at least one TLV.

Switching Granularity values are 0 (provided in signaling, see RFC 6004), 1 (Ethernet Port, for port-based service) and 2 (Ethernet Frame, for EVC-based service). The MTU is in octets and MUST NOT be smaller than 46 bytes for Ethernet v2 or 38 bytes for IEEE 802.3.

Each TLV has a 16-bit Type and a 16-bit Length that covers the whole TLV, and values are zero-padded to a multiple of four octets. Type 2 is the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile (length 24) and Type 3 is the Layer 2 Control Protocol (length 8, defined in RFC 6004). Types 0, 1 and 255 are reserved.
sections.eli5: The form has a box for what kind of link you want, a box for the biggest message size, and then a list of extra notes, each in its own labeled slot.

sections.title: The Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV
sections.content:
The Type 2 TLV carries an 8-bit Profile bit vector, an 8-bit Index, 16 reserved bits, and four 32-bit values: CIR, CBS, EIR and EBS. Profile bit 0 is the Coupling Flag and bit 1 is the Color Mode; a Color Mode of 0 means color-blind and 1 means color-aware. Other flags SHOULD be zero when sent and ignored when received. An object MAY hold more than one such TLV.

CIR and EIR are in bytes per second, CBS and EBS in bytes, all encoded as 32-bit IEEE single-precision floating-point numbers (RFC 4506). CIR and EIR MUST be at least 0. When CIR is greater than 0, CBS MUST be at least the maximum frame size, and likewise EBS when EIR is greater than 0.

The Index ties a profile to the traffic class in a multiple-class LSP and MUST match a Class-Type in the CLASSTYPE or EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object. By default it MUST be 0. One index can map to a set of class types sharing a profile, or to a single class type with a dedicated profile.
sections.eli5: This is the actual price list: how fast, how big a burst, and extra allowed speed. Each number is stored in a fixed-size slot.

sections.title: FLOWSPEC, ADSPEC and Processing Rules
sections.content:
The Ethernet FLOWSPEC object has Class-Num 9 and Class-Type 6, and the same format as the SENDER_TSPEC. There is no Ethernet ADSPEC: it is either omitted or an IntServ ADSPEC is used.

When signaling an Ethernet LSP, the Generalized LABEL_REQUEST Switching Type MUST be 51 (L2SC) and the LSP Encoding Type MUST be 2 (Ethernet). The SENDER_TSPEC SHOULD be forwarded unchanged to intermediate and egress nodes, and the FLOWSPEC flows upstream toward the ingress.

Nodes MUST check that they and their interfaces can support the requested granularity, MTU and TLV values. If not, the receiver MUST send a PathErr with error code Traffic Control Error and value Service unsupported. An MTU below the minimum Ethernet frame size gives Traffic Control Error with Bad Tspec value. A mismatch in index values with an EXTENDED_CLASSTYPE object gives Extended Class-Type Error, Class-Type mismatch.
sections.eli5: Each switch along the way checks whether it can honor the request. If it cannot, it sends back a note saying which part it could not do.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations beyond RFC 3473. GMPLS security is described in Section 11 of RFC 3471, and further details are in RFC 5920.

IANA assigned C-Type 6 under both the FLOWSPEC (class 9) and SENDER_TSPEC (class 12) classes. It created registries for Ethernet Switching Granularities, Ethernet Sender TSpec TLVs and Ethernet Bandwidth Profile bit flags (CF at 0x01 and CM at 0x02), all with Standards Action as the registration procedure.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about here beyond what the older rules already cover. The official lists were extended so that everyone uses the same numbers.

fields.name: Profile
fields.desc: Flags: bit 0 Coupling Flag, bit 1 Color Mode.

fields.name: Index
fields.desc: Refers to the traffic class; default 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent, ignored when received.
